name: fallacies_eristic
description: Informal fallacies, formal slips, statistical misreadings, and eristic stratagems — bad arguments and winning-at-any-cost tactics — each with textual cues for spotting them in a draft or an opponent's move.

relevance_fallacies.name: abusive ad hominem
relevance_fallacies.definition: Attacking the arguer's character instead of the argument, where character has no bearing on the claim.
cues: epithets attached to the source rather than the claim
relevance_fallacies.example: You would expect that argument from a dropout.

relevance_fallacies.name: guilt by association
relevance_fallacies.definition: Discrediting a claim because disliked people or groups also hold it.
relevance_fallacies.example: That's exactly what the cranks argue.

relevance_fallacies.name: genetic fallacy
relevance_fallacies.definition: Judging a claim by its origin — who invented it, where it came from — rather than its current support.
cues: etymology or founding story doing evaluative work
relevance_fallacies.example: The whole framework came out of a marketing department, so ignore it.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to unqualified authority
relevance_fallacies.definition: Citing an authority outside their field of competence, or one with no relevant expertise at all.
cues: credential mismatch ("Dr. X, a physicist, says the treatment")
celebrity endorsement of a technical claim
relevance_fallacies.example: A Nobel laureate in chemistry says the currency will collapse.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to anonymous authority
relevance_fallacies.definition: Attributing a claim to unnamed authorities or sources that cannot be checked.
relevance_fallacies.example: Studies show that most of it is wasted.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to popularity
relevance_fallacies.definition: Treating widespread belief as proof of truth.
cues: poll numbers offered on a question of fact
relevance_fallacies.example: Two-thirds of the country thinks it's unsafe, so it is.

relevance_fallacies.name: bandwagon appeal
relevance_fallacies.definition: Urging adoption because others are adopting, treating momentum as merit.
cues: adoption counts offered as quality evidence
relevance_fallacies.example: Half the industry has switched already.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to tradition
relevance_fallacies.definition: Treating long practice as sufficient justification.
relevance_fallacies.example: The department has run it this way for forty years.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to novelty
relevance_fallacies.definition: Treating newness as evidence of superiority.
relevance_fallacies.example: Nobody does it the old way anymore.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to nature
relevance_fallacies.definition: Inferring that what is natural is therefore good or safe, or that the artificial is therefore harmful.
cues: "the way it was meant to be"
relevance_fallacies.example: It's a plant extract, so it can't be toxic.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to pity
relevance_fallacies.definition: Substituting sympathy for the arguer or subject for reasons bearing on the claim.
cues: hardship narrative attached to a factual or policy conclusion
relevance_fallacies.example: The vendor put three years into the bid, so the contract should be theirs.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to force
relevance_fallacies.definition: Backing a claim with a threat of harm or sanction rather than evidence.
cues: consequences to the arguer, not to the argument
relevance_fallacies.example: People who raise that question tend not to get renewed.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to spite
relevance_fallacies.definition: Exploiting the audience's resentment of a person or group to win assent.
relevance_fallacies.example: Vote it down and watch their faces.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to flattery
relevance_fallacies.definition: Complimenting the audience so that agreement feels like a confirmation of their good sense.
relevance_fallacies.example: You're too smart to fall for the official line.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to ridicule
relevance_fallacies.definition: Presenting the opposing view in a way that makes it laughable, in place of refuting it.
cues: scare quotes around the opponent's terms
relevance_fallacies.example: So the plan is that money just appears.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to emotion
relevance_fallacies.definition: Using an affective surge — outrage, fear, tenderness — as the load-bearing support for a conclusion.
cues: vivid single-victim narrative followed by a general policy claim
relevance_fallacies.example: Look at this child's photograph and tell me the program should be cut.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to consequences
relevance_fallacies.definition: Arguing that a claim is false because its truth would be unwelcome (or true because it would be welcome).
cues: "if that were true, then" followed by an undesirable state rather than a contradiction
relevance_fallacies.example: If the reserves are that low, the town is finished — so they can't be.

relevance_fallacies.name: red herring
relevance_fallacies.definition: Argument sense: introducing a topic that is interesting but irrelevant, so that attention leaves the disputed point. Distinct from the mystery-plot red herring, which is a deliberately planted false lead.
cues: abrupt topic pivot after a hard question
answer that never touches the premise challenged
relevance_fallacies.example: Asked about the overruns, he described the site's safety record.

relevance_fallacies.name: straw man
relevance_fallacies.definition: Refuting a distorted, exaggerated, or weakened version of the opposing position.
cues: an absolute quantifier the opponent never used
relevance_fallacies.example: They want no oversight of any kind.

relevance_fallacies.name: hollow man
relevance_fallacies.definition: Attributing a position to an opponent that no identifiable opponent actually holds.
cues: "there are those who argue" with no citation
relevance_fallacies.example: Some argue the deficit doesn't exist at all.

relevance_fallacies.name: missing the point
relevance_fallacies.definition: Offering premises that support some conclusion, but not the one at issue.
cues: conclusion swells beyond the evidence's scope
argument proves an adjacent, easier claim
relevance_fallacies.example: Evidence that the program is popular is offered as evidence that it works.

relevance_fallacies.name: two wrongs make a right
relevance_fallacies.definition: Justifying a wrong by pointing to a comparable wrong by someone else.
relevance_fallacies.example: Our accounting is no worse than the competitor's.

relevance_fallacies.name: appeal to the stone
relevance_fallacies.definition: Dismissing a claim as absurd without giving any reason.
relevance_fallacies.example: That's just not serious.

relevance_fallacies.name: argument by repetition
relevance_fallacies.definition: Asserting the same claim until repetition substitutes for support.
cues: identical phrasing recurring across a piece
relevance_fallacies.example: The third time the same sentence appears, it has still not been argued.

relevance_fallacies.name: moralistic fallacy
relevance_fallacies.definition: Inferring that because something ought not to be so, it is not so.
cues: "it would be unjust if" used to deny a factual claim
relevance_fallacies.example: It would be monstrous for the disparity to be that large, so the figure must be wrong.

relevance_fallacies.name: naturalistic fallacy
relevance_fallacies.definition: Inferring an evaluative conclusion directly from purely descriptive premises.
cues: is-statements followed by ought-conclusions with no bridging value premise
"that's just how it works" as a justification
"human nature" invoked to settle a normative question
relevance_fallacies.example: Competition is how the market works, therefore it is how it should work.

ambiguity_fallacies.name: equivocation
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: A key term shifts meaning between premises so that a conclusion follows only verbally.
cues: a term appearing in two senses in one paragraph
abstract nouns like 'freedom', 'natural', 'theory' unmarked by definition
ambiguity_fallacies.example: It's only a theory — meaning conjecture in one line and scientific theory in the next.

ambiguity_fallacies.name: amphiboly
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: The ambiguity is grammatical rather than lexical: sentence structure permits two readings and the argument uses the convenient one.
cues: unclear scope of negation or coordination
ambiguity_fallacies.example: The rule bars officers and employees who hold shares — which does it modify?

ambiguity_fallacies.name: fallacy of accent
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: The meaning turns on which word is stressed, or on typographic emphasis added by the quoter.
cues: italics added by the quoting party
"we should not speak ill of our friends"-style stress games
ambiguity_fallacies.example: We do not knowingly sell defective units.

ambiguity_fallacies.name: contextomy
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: Quoting accurately but stripping context so the quotation supports the opposite of what the source meant.
cues: ellipses in the middle of a cited sentence
single clause quoted from a longer conditional
ambiguity_fallacies.example: "The results are striking" — from a sentence beginning "If replicated,".

ambiguity_fallacies.name: fallacy of composition
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: Inferring that a whole has a property because its parts do.
cues: "if it works for one, it works for all"
aggregating individually rational choices into a claim about the system
ambiguity_fallacies.example: Every household can save more, so the economy can save more.

ambiguity_fallacies.name: fallacy of division
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: Inferring that a part has a property because the whole does.
cues: group averages applied to an individual
"the industry is profitable, so this firm is"
ambiguity_fallacies.example: The class scored well, so this student did.

ambiguity_fallacies.name: reification
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: Treating an abstraction, index, or statistic as a concrete acting thing.
cues: abstractions as grammatical agents ("the market decided", "data wants")
index numbers with verbs of intention

ambiguity_fallacies.name: definist fallacy
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: Defining a contested term so that the disputed conclusion is settled by the definition.
ambiguity_fallacies.example: Since censorship means state action only, a platform ban is by definition not censorship.

ambiguity_fallacies.name: persuasive definition
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: Redefining a term with strong emotive charge to keep the charge while changing the reference.
ambiguity_fallacies.example: Real reform means cutting the budget.

ambiguity_fallacies.name: no true Scotsman
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: Rescuing a generalization from counterexamples by redefining membership to exclude them.
cues: a qualifier added only after a counterexample lands
ambiguity_fallacies.example: No serious economist believes that — after three are named.

ambiguity_fallacies.name: continuum fallacy
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: Arguing that because no precise line can be drawn, no distinction exists.
cues: "where exactly do you draw the line"
ambiguity_fallacies.example: There's no exact moment a puddle becomes a pond, so the distinction is meaningless.

ambiguity_fallacies.name: etymological fallacy
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: Insisting a word must mean what its root historically meant.
cues: "literally means" applied to settled modern usage
ambiguity_fallacies.example: 'Decimate' can only mean to reduce by a tenth.

ambiguity_fallacies.name: loki's wager
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: Refusing to allow a concept into the argument because its boundaries cannot be exactly specified.
cues: "define it precisely or we can't discuss it"
endless definitional preliminaries that never end
ambiguity_fallacies.example: Until you can say exactly which pixels are the face, we cannot talk about faces.

ambiguity_fallacies.name: weasel wording
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: Vague qualifiers create an impression of support while committing to nothing checkable.
ambiguity_fallacies.example: Users may see savings of up to forty percent.

ambiguity_fallacies.name: scope ambiguity
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: The reach of a quantifier, negation, or modal is left unfixed and the argument exploits the convenient reading.
ambiguity_fallacies.example: Everyone did not pass the audit.

ambiguity_fallacies.name: syntactic pivot on 'only'
ambiguity_fallacies.definition: Placement of a restrictive adverb changes the claim's content while the sentence reads as the same assertion.
cues: restrictive modifiers separated from what they restrict
ambiguity_fallacies.example: We only tested the units that failed / We tested only the units that failed.

presumption_fallacies.name: begging the question
presumption_fallacies.definition: The conclusion is smuggled into the premises, so the argument gives no independent reason.
cues: premise restates the conclusion in synonyms
evaluative term repeated on both sides of 'therefore'
presumption_fallacies.example: The policy is unfair because it treats people unjustly.

presumption_fallacies.name: circular reasoning
presumption_fallacies.definition: Two or more claims support each other in a closed loop with no external anchor.
cues: A cited for B and B cited for A
presumption_fallacies.example: The document is authentic because the archive accepted it; the archive accepted it because it is authentic.

presumption_fallacies.name: question-begging epithet
presumption_fallacies.definition: A loaded label does the arguing, presupposing the very evaluation at issue.
cues: adjectives like 'so-called', 'discredited', 'common-sense' attached to the disputed thing
evaluative modifier inside the noun phrase naming the issue
"this failed experiment" before any argument that it failed
presumption_fallacies.example: This discredited proposal is back before the committee.

presumption_fallacies.name: loaded question
presumption_fallacies.definition: A question whose presuppositions cannot be denied by any direct answer.
cues: yes/no question with an embedded assertion
"why do you" plus a contested predicate
presumption_fallacies.example: Why did the department hide the figures?

presumption_fallacies.name: false dilemma
presumption_fallacies.definition: Presenting two options as exhaustive when more exist.
presumption_fallacies.example: Either we deregulate or the sector dies.

presumption_fallacies.name: false equivalence
presumption_fallacies.definition: Treating two things as comparable on a dimension where they differ by an order of magnitude or in kind.
presumption_fallacies.example: A parking ticket and a felony are both breaking the law.

presumption_fallacies.name: false balance
presumption_fallacies.definition: Presenting a lopsided evidentiary dispute as an even contest by giving each side equal space.
cues: "critics say" paragraph appended to a well-evidenced finding
one dissenting expert against a literature
presumption_fallacies.example: The article gives a paragraph to the consensus and a paragraph to its only opponent.

presumption_fallacies.name: hasty generalization
presumption_fallacies.definition: Drawing a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative instances.
cues: "in my experience" plus a universal claim
case count of one or two
presumption_fallacies.example: Both start-ups I advised failed after taking outside money, so outside money kills start-ups.

presumption_fallacies.name: sweeping generalization
presumption_fallacies.definition: Applying a sound general rule to a case whose special features make it an exception.
cues: "the rule is clear" against an atypical fact pattern
presumption_fallacies.example: Exercise is healthy, so the patient in traction should run.

presumption_fallacies.name: suppressed evidence
presumption_fallacies.definition: Omitting known facts that would materially change the audience's assessment.
cues: the inconvenient year missing from a series
presumption_fallacies.example: The five-year trend is cited; the sixth year, which reverses it, is not.

presumption_fallacies.name: cherry picking
presumption_fallacies.definition: Selecting the subset of data or quotations that supports the claim and ignoring the rest.
cues: start dates chosen at a local minimum
one favorable trial out of many
presumption_fallacies.example: The chart begins in the worst month of the decade.

presumption_fallacies.name: special pleading
presumption_fallacies.definition: Applying a standard generally, then exempting one's own case without principled grounds.
cues: "this situation is different" with no stated difference
presumption_fallacies.example: Every division must cut ten percent, except the one making the argument.

presumption_fallacies.name: moving the goalposts
presumption_fallacies.definition: Raising or changing the evidentiary standard once the original standard has been met.
cues: new conditions appearing after a concession
"I'd want to see it in humans" after a human trial
presumption_fallacies.example: First one replication was demanded, then three, then a different population.

presumption_fallacies.name: unfalsifiable claim
presumption_fallacies.definition: A claim insulated so that no observation could count against it.
cues: no answer to 'what would change your mind'
presumption_fallacies.example: The absence of evidence is itself proof of the cover-up.

presumption_fallacies.name: shifting the burden of proof
presumption_fallacies.definition: Demanding the other side disprove an unsupported assertion rather than supporting it.
presumption_fallacies.example: Show me a study proving the additive is safe, or admit it isn't.

presumption_fallacies.name: argument from incredulity
presumption_fallacies.definition: Treating the arguer's inability to imagine an explanation as evidence that none exists.
presumption_fallacies.example: There's no way that happened by chance.

presumption_fallacies.name: nirvana fallacy
presumption_fallacies.definition: Rejecting a workable option because it falls short of an unattainable ideal.
cues: comparison to a perfect alternative that does not exist
presumption_fallacies.example: The screening misses some cases, so it's pointless.

presumption_fallacies.name: argument to moderation
presumption_fallacies.definition: Assuming the truth lies midway between two positions.
cues: "the truth is somewhere in the middle"
presumption_fallacies.example: One side says the bridge is sound, the other that it will collapse; call it structurally marginal.

presumption_fallacies.name: fallacy of relative privation
presumption_fallacies.definition: Dismissing a problem because a worse one exists.
presumption_fallacies.example: Why worry about outages when the grid in other countries is worse?

presumption_fallacies.name: just-world reasoning
presumption_fallacies.definition: Inferring from an outcome that the party deserved it, so no further explanation is needed.
cues: outcome offered as evidence of prior conduct
presumption_fallacies.example: The firm failed, which shows the management was bad.

presumption_fallacies.name: chronological snobbery
presumption_fallacies.definition: Assuming that a belief held earlier is discredited by the mere passage of time.
cues: "that was the thinking in the nineties"
presumption_fallacies.example: That objection dates from before the reform, so it no longer applies.

presumption_fallacies.name: thought-terminating cliche
presumption_fallacies.definition: A stock phrase deployed to close down inquiry without answering it.
presumption_fallacies.example: That's above our pay grade.

causal_fallacies.name: post hoc ergo propter hoc
causal_fallacies.definition: Inferring causation from mere temporal succession.
cues: before/after pairs with no comparison group
causal_fallacies.example: Complaints dropped after the new form went out, so the form fixed it.

causal_fallacies.name: cum hoc ergo propter hoc
causal_fallacies.definition: Inferring causation from co-occurrence or correlation alone.
causal_fallacies.example: Counties with more libraries have lower crime, so libraries cut crime.

causal_fallacies.name: reverse causation
cues: healthier subjects doing more of the exposure
outcome that plausibly precedes the supposed cause
causal_fallacies.example: Sick people use more health care, so health care makes people sick.

causal_fallacies.name: confounding
causal_fallacies.definition: Attributing to one variable an effect actually produced by a third that drives both.
cues: "controlling for" absent from an observational claim
causal_fallacies.example: Coffee drinkers get more cancer — and smoked more.

causal_fallacies.name: causal oversimplification
causal_fallacies.definition: Naming one cause for a multi-causal outcome.
cues: single-factor headline for a complex event
causal_fallacies.example: The blackout happened because of the storm.

causal_fallacies.name: joint effect
causal_fallacies.definition: Treating one effect of a common cause as the cause of another effect of it.
cues: two symptoms of one process presented as cause and effect
the earlier-appearing indicator treated as the driver
"X leads to Y" where both are outputs of the same system
causal_fallacies.example: Falling barometric pressure does not cause the storm; both come from the same system.

causal_fallacies.name: spurious correlation
causal_fallacies.definition: A statistical association arising from coincidence, shared trends, or common data processing rather than any relation.
cues: two long upward time series compared

causal_fallacies.name: slippery slope fallacy
causal_fallacies.definition: Asserting a chain of consequences without arguing any of the links.
causal_fallacies.example: Allow the exception and there will be no rule left.

causal_fallacies.name: circular cause and consequence
causal_fallacies.definition: Explaining an outcome by a cause that is itself explained by that outcome, with no independent evidence for either.
causal_fallacies.example: Neighborhoods decline because investment leaves, and investment leaves because they decline.

causal_fallacies.name: furtive fallacy
causal_fallacies.definition: Attributing outcomes to deliberate concealed agency by default.
causal_fallacies.example: The report's release date was chosen to bury it.

causal_fallacies.name: narrative fallacy
causal_fallacies.definition: Imposing a coherent causal story on outcomes that were substantially driven by chance or unmeasured factors.
cues: post-mortems where every event has a reason
causal_fallacies.example: The company failed because of the 2019 rebrand.

causal_fallacies.name: magical thinking
causal_fallacies.definition: Positing a causal link on grounds of resemblance, contagion, or symbolic association.
cues: "sends a message" as a causal mechanism
causal_fallacies.example: Renaming the program restores public trust.

causal_fallacies.name: cargo cult reasoning
causal_fallacies.definition: Copying the surface features of a successful process while omitting the mechanism that made it work.
cues: "best practice" transplants with no theory of why
causal_fallacies.example: Adopting the standup meeting without the delivery discipline around it.

causal_fallacies.name: ignoring counterfactual baseline
causal_fallacies.definition: Crediting an intervention with a change that would have happened anyway.
cues: attribution of secular trends to a policy
causal_fallacies.example: Sales rose after the campaign — as they do every fourth quarter.

statistical_fallacies.name: base-rate neglect
statistical_fallacies.definition: Judging a probability from the specific evidence while ignoring how common the condition is to begin with.
statistical_fallacies.example: A 99%-accurate test for a 1-in-10,000 condition still yields mostly false positives.

statistical_fallacies.name: prosecutor's fallacy
statistical_fallacies.definition: Confusing the probability of the evidence given innocence with the probability of innocence given the evidence.
cues: "the chance of a random match is one in a million, so"
statistical_fallacies.example: One-in-a-million match odds treated as one-in-a-million odds of innocence.

statistical_fallacies.name: defense attorney's fallacy
statistical_fallacies.definition: Dismissing probabilistic evidence because many people share the trait, ignoring the other evidence that narrows the pool.
cues: evidence evaluated in isolation from the case
statistical_fallacies.example: Ten thousand men in the city wear that size, so the print means nothing.

statistical_fallacies.name: denominator neglect
statistical_fallacies.definition: Presenting counts without the population they came from.
cues: raw counts across differently sized groups
statistical_fallacies.example: More accidents happen on clear days than in fog.

statistical_fallacies.name: denominator switching
statistical_fallacies.definition: Changing the base between comparisons so the numbers are no longer commensurable.
cues: "of those surveyed" vs. "of all customers" in adjacent sentences
statistical_fallacies.example: Forty percent of respondents and twenty percent of the population, compared as if equal.

statistical_fallacies.name: relative risk inflation
statistical_fallacies.definition: Reporting a relative change to make a tiny absolute change sound large.
cues: "a fifty percent increase" without the baseline rate
statistical_fallacies.example: Risk rises from two in a million to four in a million: a 100% increase.

statistical_fallacies.name: ecological fallacy
statistical_fallacies.definition: Inferring an individual-level relationship from group-level data.
cues: district or country averages used to describe persons
statistical_fallacies.example: Richer counties vote a certain way, so richer people do.

statistical_fallacies.name: atomistic fallacy
statistical_fallacies.definition: Inferring a group-level relationship from individual-level data, ignoring context effects.
statistical_fallacies.example: Individual tutoring works, therefore universal tutoring would raise national scores proportionally.

statistical_fallacies.name: simpson's paradox misreading
statistical_fallacies.definition: Reporting an aggregate association that reverses within every subgroup, or the reverse.
statistical_fallacies.example: Both departments admit women at higher rates; the university appears to admit men at higher rates.

statistical_fallacies.name: regression fallacy
statistical_fallacies.definition: Attributing to an intervention an improvement that is regression to the mean from an extreme starting point.
statistical_fallacies.example: The clinics with the worst quarter improved after the visit — as they would have anyway.

statistical_fallacies.name: survivorship bias
statistical_fallacies.definition: Drawing conclusions from the cases that remained visible while the ones that disappeared are unobserved.
statistical_fallacies.example: Studying returning bombers' damage rather than the ones that never returned.

statistical_fallacies.name: selection bias
statistical_fallacies.definition: The sample is assembled in a way that makes it unrepresentative of the target population.
statistical_fallacies.example: An online poll of a site's own readers reported as national opinion.

statistical_fallacies.name: berkson's paradox
statistical_fallacies.definition: Conditioning on a selection criterion creates a spurious negative association between two independent traits.
cues: correlations computed within a filtered population
statistical_fallacies.example: Among admitted patients, two unrelated diseases appear inversely related.

statistical_fallacies.name: texas sharpshooter fallacy
statistical_fallacies.definition: Drawing the target around the cluster: defining the hypothesis after seeing where the data fell.
statistical_fallacies.example: Cancer cases cluster in this block — as some block must be highest.

statistical_fallacies.name: multiple comparisons neglect
statistical_fallacies.definition: Reporting a significant result from many tests without correcting for the number of chances to find one.
cues: long subgroup tables with one starred cell
statistical_fallacies.example: One of twenty outcomes reached p < 0.05.

statistical_fallacies.name: p-hacking
statistical_fallacies.definition: Trying analytic variants until one crosses a significance threshold, then reporting only that one.
statistical_fallacies.example: Results held after dropping the two 'outlier' sites.

statistical_fallacies.name: harking
statistical_fallacies.definition: HARKing — hypothesizing after the results are known: presenting a hypothesis formed after seeing the data as if it had been predicted in advance.
cues: exploratory findings written up as confirmatory
statistical_fallacies.example: The paper's stated hypothesis matches the one subgroup that worked.
statistical_fallacies.aka: hypothesizing after the results are known

statistical_fallacies.name: publication bias
statistical_fallacies.definition: Treating the published literature as the evidence base when null results were less likely to be published.
cues: no funnel plot or registry check
statistical_fallacies.example: Twelve published trials are positive; the registry lists thirty.

statistical_fallacies.name: law of small numbers
statistical_fallacies.definition: Expecting small samples to show the properties of large ones, so noise reads as signal.
cues: rankings of small units (counties, schools, clinics)
"the highest rate in the country" for a tiny population
statistical_fallacies.example: The smallest counties have both the highest and the lowest cancer rates.

statistical_fallacies.name: gambler's fallacy
statistical_fallacies.definition: Believing independent trials must self-correct in the short run.
statistical_fallacies.example: Red has come up six times, so black is overdue.

statistical_fallacies.name: conjunction fallacy
statistical_fallacies.definition: Judging a conjunction more probable than one of its conjuncts because the story is more representative.
cues: a detailed scenario preferred over a general one
statistical_fallacies.example: Bank teller and activist rated likelier than bank teller.

statistical_fallacies.name: spurious precision
statistical_fallacies.definition: Reporting more significant figures than the measurement can support.
statistical_fallacies.example: The forecast puts the loss at $1,283,417.

statistical_fallacies.name: extrapolation beyond the data
statistical_fallacies.definition: Projecting a fitted relationship past the range where it was observed.
cues: straight lines extended off the chart
statistical_fallacies.example: At the current rate of improvement, times will fall below zero by the next century.

statistical_fallacies.name: mean-median conflation
statistical_fallacies.definition: Using the average where a skewed distribution makes it unrepresentative.
statistical_fallacies.example: Average salary at the firm rises when one executive is hired.

statistical_fallacies.name: mcnamara fallacy
statistical_fallacies.definition: Treating what is measured as the whole of what matters and discarding the rest.
statistical_fallacies.example: Body counts as the metric of progress.

statistical_fallacies.name: false negative neglect
statistical_fallacies.definition: Reading a negative test or null result as proof of absence without regard to power or sensitivity.
cues: no power calculation or detection limit
statistical_fallacies.example: A trial of forty patients found no difference, so there is none.

statistical_fallacies.name: misleading axis framing
statistical_fallacies.definition: Chart construction — truncated axes, dual scales, cumulative totals — creates an impression the data do not support.
cues: y-axis not starting at zero on a bar chart
cumulative curves that can only rise
statistical_fallacies.example: A two-point move fills the whole chart.

statistical_fallacies.name: unadjusted comparison
statistical_fallacies.definition: Comparing groups or periods without adjusting for composition, inflation, or population change.
cues: crude rates across differently aged populations
statistical_fallacies.example: Ticket sales in dollars are at a record — before adjusting for prices.

formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.name: affirming the consequent
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.definition: From 'if P then Q' and Q, concluding P.
cues: "if it were X, we'd see Y — and we see Y"
diagnostic reasoning without ruling out alternatives
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.example: If it rained, the street is wet; the street is wet, so it rained.

formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.name: denying the antecedent
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.definition: From 'if P then Q' and not-P, concluding not-Q.
cues: "since we didn't do X, Y won't happen"
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.example: If you overtrain you get injured; she didn't overtrain, so she isn't injured.

formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.name: undistributed middle
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.definition: Two categories share a middle term that is never taken in its full extent, so no link follows.
cues: shared attribute used to equate classes
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.example: Frauds use spreadsheets; this firm uses spreadsheets.

formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.name: illicit major
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.definition: The predicate term is distributed in the conclusion but not in the premise.
cues: universal negative conclusion from a particular premise
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.example: All auditors are careful; no clerks are auditors; so no clerks are careful.

formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.name: illicit minor
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.definition: The subject term is distributed in the conclusion but not in the premise.
cues: conclusion covering the whole class when the premise covered only some
"all" in the conclusion where the premise said "all X are Y" the other way round
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.example: All accountants are trained; all accountants are employees; so all employees are trained.

formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.name: fallacy of four terms
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.definition: A syllogism uses four distinct terms because one word carries two senses.
cues: a repeated word with shifting reference
technical and lay senses of one term in one argument
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.example: Nothing is better than wisdom; a dry crust is better than nothing.

formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.name: existential fallacy
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.definition: Deriving a claim that something exists from premises that are purely universal.
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.example: All unicorns are horned, so some horned things are unicorns.

formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.name: quantifier shift
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.definition: Swapping the order of quantifiers, turning 'each has some' into 'some serves all'.
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.example: Everyone has a mother, therefore someone is everyone's mother.

formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.name: affirming a disjunct
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.definition: From 'P or Q' and P, concluding not-Q, when the disjunction is inclusive.
cues: "it's either A or B" followed by exclusion
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.example: The failure was hardware or software; it was hardware, so not software.

formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.name: denying a conjunct
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.definition: From 'not both P and Q' and not-P, concluding Q.
cues: "we can't have both" plus one denial
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.example: We can't have both speed and cheapness; it isn't fast, so it's cheap.

formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.name: masked man fallacy
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.definition: Substituting co-referring terms inside a belief or knowledge context, where substitution is not valid.
cues: "he doesn't know that X is Y, therefore"
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.example: She knows her colleague; she doesn't know the whistleblower; so her colleague isn't the whistleblower.

formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.name: modal scope fallacy
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.definition: Confusing the necessity of a conditional with the necessity of its consequent.
cues: "must" migrating from the inference to the fact
formal_and_probabilistic_fallacies.example: If he is running, he must be moving — so he must be moving.

eristic_stratagems.name: extension
eristic_stratagems.definition: Stretching the opponent's claim beyond its stated limits so that a wider, weaker version can be refuted.
eristic_stratagems.example: He said the policy usually helps; it is answered as if he claimed it always helps.

eristic_stratagems.name: homonymy
eristic_stratagems.definition: Deliberately exploiting a second sense of the opponent's word to refute something they never said.
eristic_stratagems.example: 'Honour' as reputation answered with 'honour' as virtue.

eristic_stratagems.name: absolutizing the relative
eristic_stratagems.definition: Taking a claim made under a stated condition and refuting it as if made unconditionally.
cues: stripped 'in this context' or 'for these patients'
eristic_stratagems.example: "Under sedation the drug is safe" answered with cases of unsedated harm.
eristic_stratagems.aka: a dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter

eristic_stratagems.name: concealing the conclusion
eristic_stratagems.definition: Obtaining assent to premises one at a time, in scattered order, so the opponent cannot see what is being built.
cues: questions asked out of logical sequence
long strings of small agreements before any conclusion appears
eristic_stratagems.example: Six unconnected concessions later, the conclusion is announced as already granted.

eristic_stratagems.name: arguing from false premises the opponent accepts
eristic_stratagems.definition: Using premises one believes false because the opponent is committed to them.
cues: premises the arguer would reject in another context
eristic_stratagems.example: Using an opponent's ranking system to derive a conclusion the arguer does not otherwise endorse.

eristic_stratagems.name: provoking anger
eristic_stratagems.definition: Irritating the opponent so their judgment degrades and they overstate.
eristic_stratagems.example: Steady condescension until the opponent says something indefensible.

eristic_stratagems.name: rapid-fire questioning
eristic_stratagems.definition: Asking many questions quickly so that answers cannot be considered and confusion looks like concession.
eristic_stratagems.example: Five questions in one breath, then a claim that none were answered.

eristic_stratagems.name: diversion
eristic_stratagems.definition: When losing on the point, changing the subject to one where the arguer is stronger.
cues: topic shift immediately after a concession
eristic_stratagems.example: Cornered on the number, he moves to the moral stakes.

eristic_stratagems.name: generalizing the granted instance
eristic_stratagems.definition: Treating a single conceded case as an admission of the general rule.
cues: one example escalated to a principle
eristic_stratagems.example: He conceded one exception, and is told he has conceded the class.

eristic_stratagems.name: argumentum ad auditores
eristic_stratagems.definition: Aiming an invalid but plausible-sounding objection at the audience rather than the opponent, knowing the audience cannot check it.
eristic_stratagems.example: A jargon-laden objection lands with spectators though it means nothing to the specialist.

eristic_stratagems.name: appeal to an authority the opponent reveres
eristic_stratagems.definition: Quoting a source the opponent cannot repudiate without cost, whether or not it is relevant.
cues: scripture, founding documents, or a revered figure quoted at a technical dispute
eristic_stratagems.example: Citing the opponent's own mentor against them.

eristic_stratagems.name: declaring the point beyond the opponent
eristic_stratagems.definition: Dismissing an objection as too advanced or too specialized for the objector to evaluate.
cues: "you'd need the background to see why"
"this is settled among people who work on it"
eristic_stratagems.example: The question is waved off as naive rather than answered.

eristic_stratagems.name: bewildering with words
eristic_stratagems.definition: Burying a weak position in unintelligible verbiage so that the audience assumes there is content.
cues: unusually long sentences at exactly the weak point
eristic_stratagems.example: Three clauses of terminology where a number belongs.

eristic_stratagems.name: retorsion
eristic_stratagems.definition: Turning the opponent's own argument back so that it tells against their position.
cues: mirrored structure of the opponent's sentence
eristic_stratagems.example: If disclosure is dangerous, so is your own undisclosed proposal.

eristic_stratagems.name: claiming victory on an unproven point
eristic_stratagems.definition: Announcing that a point has been established and proceeding as if it were settled.
eristic_stratagems.example: The summary asserts a conclusion the body never supported.

eristic_stratagems.name: interrupting the derivation
eristic_stratagems.definition: Breaking off the discussion or forcing a recess when the opponent's argument is about to close.
cues: procedural objections at the decisive step
eristic_stratagems.example: The clock is invoked one question before the conclusion.

eristic_stratagems.name: anticipatory objection
eristic_stratagems.definition: Refuting an argument before the opponent has stated it, in a weakened form of one's own making.
eristic_stratagems.example: Their objection is stated for them, badly, and dismissed.

eristic_stratagems.name: arguing to exhaustion
eristic_stratagems.definition: Prolonging the exchange until the opponent yields from fatigue rather than conviction.
cues: very long replies to short objections
eristic_stratagems.example: The tenth round of the same objection, reworded.

eristic_stratagems.name: insisting on a yes-or-no answer
eristic_stratagems.definition: Forcing a binary answer to a question whose honest answer requires a distinction.
eristic_stratagems.example: Answer yes or no: has the program wasted money?

eristic_stratagems.name: false concession
eristic_stratagems.definition: Granting a trivial point loudly so that the appearance of fairness covers refusal on the real one.
cues: concession followed by 'but' and the original position intact
eristic_stratagems.example: He concedes a date error and repeats the disputed claim unchanged.

eristic_stratagems.name: personal escalation
eristic_stratagems.definition: When the argument is lost, abandoning the subject and attacking the person.
eristic_stratagems.example: The last exchange is entirely about the opponent's motives.

eristic_stratagems.name: manufactured technicality
eristic_stratagems.definition: Disputing a minor formal point to avoid the substantive one.
cues: objections about terminology or citation format
eristic_stratagems.example: The response addresses only the misuse of a word in the question.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: motte-and-bailey
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Advancing a controversial claim, then retreating under challenge to a nearly unobjectionable one and treating its defense as vindicating the first.
cues: the defended claim differing from the asserted one
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: The strong causal claim in the headline becomes 'it's worth studying' under questioning.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: gish gallop
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Overwhelming with a rapid volume of assertions, so that refuting each costs more than making them.
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: Thirty claims in four minutes, each requiring an hour to check.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: sealioning
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Persistent, superficially polite demands for evidence and explanation used to exhaust rather than to learn.
cues: "I'm just asking for a source" repeated
questions that reset after each answer
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: Every answer produces the same request, rephrased.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: just asking questions
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Insinuating a claim through interrogatives while disclaiming any assertion.
cues: questions with no interest in answers
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: Why has nobody explained the timing? — asserting a cover-up without asserting it.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: whataboutism
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Deflecting criticism by raising a counter-accusation instead of answering.
cues: immediate pivot to the critic's side's conduct
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: Asked about the fine, the reply lists the regulator's failures.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: darvo
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Denying the conduct, attacking the person who raised it, and reversing victim and offender roles.
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: The accused announces that the accusation has destroyed their life, and stops there.
rhetorical_dark_patterns.aka: deny, attack, reverse victim and offender

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: concern trolling
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Undermining a position while posing as a sympathetic supporter worried about tactics or optics.
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: A supporter's letter that advises abandoning the only effective demand.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: tone policing
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Rejecting an argument on grounds of the manner in which it was made.
cues: focus on delivery after a substantive point
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: The reply addresses the adjective and not the finding.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: isolated demand for rigor
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Applying a demanding evidentiary standard to one claim while accepting comparable claims freely.
cues: methodological objections raised only against unwelcome results
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: The unwelcome study needs replication; the welcome one is a press release.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: kafkatrap
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Structuring the charge so that denial is treated as confirmation.
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: Objecting to the accusation is entered as evidence for it.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: nutpicking
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Representing a group by its least defensible members.
cues: screenshots of anonymous accounts as evidence about a movement
"this is what they believe" over a fringe example
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: A random comment stands in for a professional literature.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: firehose of falsehood
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: High-volume, multichannel, mutually inconsistent claims that aim at exhaustion and cynicism rather than belief.
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: Four incompatible explanations issued in a week, none withdrawn.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: dog whistle
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Phrasing that reads as innocuous to a general audience while carrying a specific message to an in-group.
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: A term with an innocent surface meaning and a well-known second reading.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: manufactured controversy
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Generating the appearance of live scientific or factual dispute to delay action.
cues: debate framing over an unbalanced literature
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: Two decades of 'more research is needed' from one funded lab.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: sanewashing
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Restating an incoherent or extreme statement in reasonable terms it did not have, then defending the improved version.
cues: paraphrase far more coherent than the quotation
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: A rambling remark is reported as a considered policy position.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: strategic ambiguity
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Wording chosen so that two audiences hear incompatible commitments and neither can quote a broken promise.
cues: no deadline, no agent, no number
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: We remain committed to addressing the concerns raised.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: preemptive victim framing
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Positioning any coming criticism as persecution, so that criticism confirms the frame.
cues: "they'll come after me for saying this"
"you're not allowed to say" before saying it
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: The claim opens by predicting censorship it never encounters.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: burden inversion by asymmetric caution
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Demanding proof of safety from one side while assuming safety on the other, without stating the asymmetry.
cues: precaution invoked in one direction only
"until we know for certain" applied selectively
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: The new option must prove harmlessness; the status quo need not.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: flooding the record
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Burying the decisive item in volume — thousands of pages, exhaustive disclosure, endless caveats.
cues: material fact in an appendix footnote
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: The disclosure is complete and unreadable.

rhetorical_dark_patterns.name: false consensus signaling
rhetorical_dark_patterns.definition: Asserting that agreement already exists so that dissent looks eccentric.
rhetorical_dark_patterns.example: The claim's contested status is dissolved by a clause.
